job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Amira Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, tell me about a normal day right now, in your job hunt, your first job or your studies.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a trainee site engineer for a road and drainage contractor in Nottingham. I started in August, so three months. I wear boots and a hi-vis vest most days, set out levels with the surveyor, check measurements of trenches, and do the daily diary and quantity sheets back in the cabin. I studied civil engineering at university here, passed with an average result, and never got a placement because I was caring for my gran two days a week. I rent a room in a shared house with two nurses. I go to church on Sundays and sing in the choir. I use an AI chatbot now and then to tidy my reports, but my site manager Dennis checks everything with a red pen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I'd expected, since a road still has to be dug by somebody. At work I'd tell Dennis the chatbot helps with my diary entries and not much else. To friends at church I'd say good, we can all carry on. Online I'd say not much, I'm not a great one for posting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, my work stays the same and so do my money worries. I pay off a huge loan, my room costs a lot, and I've less than a month's money saved. The contractor lives on council road contracts, and if the council cuts a budget, we lose work. That's what I'd worry about, and it's nothing to do with AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am and say yes to overtime and extra site hours, because the site pays a little more for weekends. I'd save £70 a month. I'd keep using the chatbot for reports, but I'd check them. And I'd keep helping my gran on Sundays, because I'd never skip that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels okay. I'd say steady. A tiny bit tight in the chest, because of the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned caring for your gran. How does that fit with a full-time job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She lives two streets from my room. I pop in before work and on Sundays after choir. My mum lives an hour away and does the rest. It's tiring, but it's what you do for family. Dennis lets me start late on Mondays to take her to the clinic, which I'm grateful for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the council cuts a contract?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dennis told us two years ago they lost a drainage job and let four people go, mostly the newest. I'd be the newest. I'd look straight away for work with a utility company or a housebuilder, because they need site engineers. I'd also ask the chapel's job club for tips. It's a worry, but I'd survive.

say: I'd say it's what I expected, since a road still has to be **dug** by somebody.
I'd tell Dennis (my site manager) the chatbot helps with my **diary** entries and little else.
think: My work and **money** worries stay the same, with a huge loan and under a month saved.
The firm lives on **council** contracts, so a budget cut could cost me my job.
do: Take **overtime** and weekend site hours for extra pay.
Keep helping my **gran** on Sundays after choir.
feel: Steady, with a tiny bit tight in the **chest** because of the money.
S0.quote: A road still has to be dug by somebody.
fieldNote: Her worry is **council** budgets and being the newest, learned from a past layoff.
Caring for her gran shapes her time and her sense of duty.
She downplays fear, a mark of her steady, dutiful style.

steps.text: Take weekend overtime on site for extra pay
Save £70 a month from each pay cheque
Ask the church job club about utility and housebuilder vacancies

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's changing the office side of construction, and I can see it already. At work I'd tell Dennis that the quantity sheets and scheduling are the first things the software will do. To friends I'd say I'm not too worried because someone has to be on the ground. Online, nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, a chunk of my job is exactly what AI takes: quantity sheets, diary, tender documents. Dennis uses a new planning programme and it's already faster than the planner. The site work, setting out and checking, stays. So I think the job survives but there'll be fewer of us. I'd be sad if my group of three juniors went to two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend more time on site and less in the cabin, to be the person who's out there. I'd use the AI tools more, to keep up with what the office does. I'd study for the professional institution exams, in the evenings, since being chartered protects a career. And I'd keep my costs down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a quiet shift. Not frightening, but I notice it. I'd say mostly steady and a little watchful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does being chartered protect you from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From being seen as a pair of hands. A chartered engineer signs off safety on a drainage run, and that's a legal responsibility a machine can't hold. It takes about four years and a lot of paperwork. It's also respected, like a trade qualification, which matters to my family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bev (the office administrator) who types up the quantity sheets by hand. She's fifty-eight, and the software does her job in minutes. She's lovely, she brings in cake on Fridays. Nobody's said a word to her yet, and I find that hard to watch.

I'd say I'm not too worried because someone has to be on the **ground**.
think: A chunk of my job, **quantity sheets**, diary and tenders, is what AI takes.
The job survives but there'll be **fewer** of us.

Study for the professional **institution** exams in the evenings.
Use AI tools more to keep up with the **office** side.
feel: A quiet shift, not frightening, mostly steady and a little **watchful**.
S1.quote: A chartered engineer signs off safety on a drainage run, and that's a legal responsibility a machine can't hold.
fieldNote: She reads her own **task list** precisely and picks the site side as protection.
Chartered status is both career insurance and family pride.
Concern for office administrator Bev shows her loyalty.

steps.text: Spend three days a week on site instead of the cabin
Study evenings for the institution's chartered engineer exams
Use the AI tools for diary and quantity sheets, then check them

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is a shock, and that it'd be hard for everyone. At work I'd ask Dennis what the company will do. To friends at church I'd say pray, save and help each other. Online I'd say nothing, but I'd go to a meeting if someone organised one, since people ought to be talking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think the thinking half of my job goes within two years. The contractor wouldn't need the planners, and probably not the juniors who do paperwork. It'd leave the site side, but I'm so new I'd be the one let go. Then robots come around 2031, and there'd be three years of mud and pipes where people are still needed. I'm scared, but I'd rather be on a site than behind a desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to be moved on to site full-time and get my tickets, like the plant machinery and safety certificates. I'd move back into my mum's house for a bit, to save on the room. I'd cut everything. I'd ask my church friends to look out for work, because we help each other. And I'd study for the chartered exams anyway, because I'm stubborn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels heavy. I'd say a bit alarmed, and a bit angry that no one in charge seems to be saying anything useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your mum say about you coming home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say about time, honestly. She'd make my old room up, and she'd feed me. She'd also tell me off for not asking sooner. We're not rich, but we'd get through it. My dad would pretend not to be worried and he'd be on the phone to his friends about jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame for the situation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not Dennis, he's been fair. I'd blame the big companies that rush this out, and the politicians who don't prepare us. But mostly I'd say, what's the use. I've got to get on with it. That's how I was brought up.

say: I'd say two years is a **shock**, and ask Dennis what the company will do.
I'd tell church friends to pray, save and help each **other**.
think: The thinking half of my job goes within two years, and as the **newest** I'd be let go.
Robots come around 2031, so there are three years of **mud and pipes** where people are needed.
do: Ask to move **full-time** onto site and get plant and safety tickets.
Move back into my **mum's** house to save on the room.
Ask church friends to look out for **work**, and keep studying for chartered exams.
feel: Heavy, a bit alarmed and **angry** that nobody in charge says anything useful.
S2.quote: I'd rather be on a site than behind a desk.
fieldNote: She understands the **3-year** robot lag and chooses the site as her ground.
Mum's spare room and church friends are her net, offered without fuss.
She blames companies and politicians, not her boss.

steps.text: Ask Dennis to move me onto site full-time
Get plant machinery and safety tickets this year
Move back into my mum's house and stop paying for the room
Ask my church friends to look out for site jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, so let's get on with it. At work I'd ask Dennis to plan the company's training so juniors learn to do site work and the new tools. To friends at church I'd say we should teach the young ones a skill. Online I'd say governments should back apprenticeships, because that's how you get people into proper work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm not afraid, but I'm careful. Five years lets me do the chartered exams, and maybe save a deposit. I don't expect the site to be empty by 2031, and the robots take longer. I'd like to be the person who uses the AI planning tools, so they don't shove me aside. I'd also like to marry one day, and I want a steady income when I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the chartered exams, save £100 a month, and ask for a move into planning and site management. I'd learn the AI planning software properly. I'd keep up the choir and my gran. And I'd try to buy a small flat in about six years, maybe with my sister if she's willing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels manageable. There's a bit of pride in that I'm already doing the things I'd planned. I'd call myself mostly calm, with some nerves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a move into planning and site management?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the planner's job is the one AI is eating, and the site manager's isn't. If I'm both, I can use the tools and still be the one in boots. Dennis told me that a manager who can read a drawing and a programme is rare. I'd like to be rare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the five years went by and nothing changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have a better qualification, some savings and a better job. That's not wasted. Honestly, I'd rather be over-prepared than under. My mum says to prepare for rain even on a dry day.

say: I'd ask Dennis to plan **training** so juniors learn site work and the new tools.
think: I'm not afraid but I'm **careful**, with time for the chartered exams and a deposit.
I want a steady **income** for when I marry one day.
do: Finish the **chartered** exams and save £100 a month.
Move into planning and **site management** and learn the AI planning software.
Buy a small **flat** in about six years, maybe with my sister.
feel: Manageable, with a bit of **pride** and some nerves.
S3.quote: My mum says to prepare for rain even on a dry day.
fieldNote: Five years supports a **concrete** ladder: exams, planning role, savings.
Her aim is to be both tool-user and site-ready.
Marriage and family sit quietly behind her saving.

steps.text: Pass the chartered engineer exams within four years
Save £100 a month towards a flat deposit
Learn the AI planning software and ask for a planning role
Plan a flat purchase with my sister in six years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and we should use it to teach the young ones well. At work I'd say let's keep a proper apprenticeship scheme going. To friends I'd say not to fear it. Online I'd say governments should make it easy to retrain, and not spend the money on handouts that don't lead anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm pretty calm. I'd have a career, a chartered qualification, and maybe be a site manager. I'd be married by then, I hope, and have a child. The machines may change how things are done, but I think people will still be in charge of the safety side. That's what I'm betting on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd become chartered, move up to site manager, and buy a flat with my savings. I'd keep singing in the choir, and keep caring for my gran as long as she lives. I'd help set up a training scheme for school-leavers, if the firm would let me. And I'd keep an eye on what AI can do, so I'm never behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels good. I'd say calm, even a bit cheerful. I'm still a worrier about money, but not about the future in general.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're betting on safety. What if you're wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd have to move into something else, and I've got ten years to do it. I'd rather bet on something based on law and responsibility than something based on speed. If it goes wrong, I can retrain. I'm not afraid of trying again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want in a training scheme for school-leavers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Real wages, a mentor who's not too busy, and a chance to do actual work in the first week. And the chance to learn the new tools alongside the old ways. I'd also want girls on it. I was one of four women in my year of sixty.

say: I'd say ten years is long, so let's **teach** the young ones well.
I'd tell friends not to **fear** it.
think: I'm pretty **calm**: a chartered qualification, maybe a site manager, maybe married.
People will still be in charge of the **safety** side, and that's what I'm betting on.
do: Become **chartered** and move up to site manager.
Help set up a training scheme for **school-leavers**.
Keep **caring** for my gran and singing in the choir.
feel: Good, calm and even a bit **cheerful**, still a worrier about money.
S4.quote: I'd rather bet on something based on law and responsibility than something based on speed.
fieldNote: Her calm comes from a **bet** on safety work, which she can defend and has a plan B for.
She wants to widen the door for other young women.
Traditional values show in duty, family and marriage.

steps.text: Become a chartered engineer and move up to site manager
Help the firm set up a paid scheme for school-leavers
Save for a flat and wedding costs
Keep caring for my gran and singing in the choir

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it takes away the paperwork half of the job before I've proven myself. I'd be the newest, with a loan and not much saved. What would help is a clear plan from the company, a paid route onto the site side, and something to cover my rent while I switch.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people think graduates in construction have it easy. I wear a hi-vis vest in the rain and still owe a fortune for a piece of paper. I'm not complaining, I like it, but I'd like someone to say that it's hard and it's fair to say so.

headlineQuote: I wear a hi-vis vest in the rain and still owe a fortune for a piece of paper.
portrait: Amira is a 22-year-old civil engineering graduate working as a **trainee site engineer** for a road contractor in Nottingham.
She is traditional and steady: she sings in a church choir, cares for her gran, and uses AI now and then.
She has heavy debt, under a month saved and no family money, so **council** contract risks worry her.
She sees the site side as protection and plans for chartered status.
Two years alarms her, while ten years leaves her calm and ready to train others.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture, because the paperwork half goes first and she's the newest.
whatWouldHelp: A clear plan from the company, a paid route to **site work**, and help with rent while she switches.
